![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14227024/assets/08c3195e7325d853f61562b1f62460cb0796f14377286228f2b7cd40983202ac.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=3\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$  traversed from the point $A(4,0)$ to the point $B(0,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =3\,i+\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\,i+\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =3\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-12\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\,dt \\  & =[12\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(0+\frac{\pi }{2})-(12+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-12\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-1)\,dt \\  & ={-t|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+9}$ traversed from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(4,5).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\,j,\,0\le t\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9})j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\,j)\cdot (i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\,j) \\  & =t\cdot 1+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}} \\  & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}2t\,dt \\  & ={t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $y={e}^{2x}$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,{e}^{2})?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=t\,i+{e}^{2t}\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+{e}^{2t}\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={e}^{2t}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={x}^{2}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2t}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})j \\  & =i+2{e}^{2t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (i+2{e}^{2t}\,j) \\  & ={t}^{2}\cdot 1+2t\cdot 2{e}^{2t} \\  & ={t}^{2}+4t{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}+4t{e}^{2t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t(t+4{e}^{2t})\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=-x\,i+y\,j$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+y\,j \\  & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =32\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,dt \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-8+8 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$
